description: We built Wander, a public web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Type any star or coordinates and watch that patch of sky change across every NASA SPHEREx pass, like a flipbook. It catches moving stars like Barnard's Star, shows WISE 0855 glowing in the infrared, and builds spectra and light curves on the fly, all checked against NASA catalogues. We work in Python (Astropy), React and WebGL, and welcome anyone into astronomy, data visualization or design.
summary: Wander is a public web tool that turns any patch of sky into a flipbook of NASA SPHEREx observations, so anyone can spot things that move or change. Type a star name or coordinates and Wander queries NASA's IRSA archive live, reads only the needed pixels from each SPHEREx exposure, aligns them to one grid and stacks them per pass and per detector. You can blink between passes, subtract them so moving stars become dark/bright pairs, stack them, sweep through SPHEREx's 102 infrared colours, or view the data as a 3D cube. Spectra and light curves are measured on the fly. On the challenge targets it recovers Barnard's Star's motion (1.58 px measured vs 1.64 px predicted), shows WISE 0855 dominating only at 4–5 µm, and tracks R Draconis's pulsation. Field-star fluxes agree with NASA's 2MASS and AllWISE catalogues to about 2%. Every view has a shareable, embeddable link.
details:
What it does: Wander shows how a patch of sky changes across every SPHEREx pass. Enter a name or RA/Dec, choose a field of view, and watch a WebGL flipbook of the sky. Modes: Blink, Difference (movers become dark/bright pairs), Swipe, Stack (deeper), a 102-colour sweep, and 3D cubes (time or wavelength). Click any star for its spectrum; light curves compare only matching wavelengths, because SPHEREx's filter changes colour across the detector.

How it works: a Python/FastAPI pipeline queries IRSA's TAP service live (no hardcoded data release), reads only the needed pixels from each Level 2 file with HTTP byte ranges (verified pixel-identical to IRSA's cutouts), subtracts zodiacal light, masks contaminated pixels by flag name, propagates proper motions, reprojects to a common grid, and builds inverse-variance coadds per detector and pass. Photometry uses each exposure's official ePSF and the Solid Angle Pixel Map.

Accuracy: field-star fluxes match NASA's 2MASS and AllWISE catalogues within 4–6% in every band (median 2.4%); positions match to 0.16″; measured motions match catalogue proper motions in size and direction. 51 automated tests and a validation report ship with the code.

Impact: it makes a professional survey usable by students and the public, like the blink comparator that found Pluto, now with 102 colours.

Tools: Python, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, photutils, NumPy, FastAPI; TypeScript, React, WebGL2, three.js, D3, Aladin Lite. Hosted on Vercel and Render.

Code: https://github.com/ADITYAGABA1322/Wander

Use of AI: we used an AI coding assistant to help write parts of the code and documentation. All scientific results were checked by us against NASA data.
